questions.q: A young man promised to give up a harmful habit, saying “I will do it.” What did the author tell him to say instead?
options: “I will ask for help”
Not quite. The article says: “I have done it”.
“I have done it”
Yes. The principle is “now or never.”
“I need more time”
Not quite. The article says: “I have done it”.
“I shall try my best”
Not quite. The article says: “I have done it”.
questions.rationale: “‘I will do it’ is a kind of luxury which we cannot afford. We have to take decisions at once.”

questions.q: Fear of a cobra makes anyone act instantly. What does the editorial say a wise person does with this fact?
options: Keeps himself always afraid
Not quite. The article says: Learns to call up the same alertness of mind without needing fear.
Learns to call up the same alertness of mind without needing fear
Right. That is what sets man apart from animals.
Avoids every dangerous place
Not quite. The article says: Learns to call up the same alertness of mind without needing fear.
Uses fear to motivate others
Not quite. The article says: Learns to call up the same alertness of mind without needing fear.
questions.rationale: “What differentiates a human being from an animal is that man should be able to activate the potentials in his mind without fear.”

questions.q: The article compares a member of society to the driver of a steam engine standing by the fire. What is the comparison?
options: He must control both his anger at others and his wish to run away, so that society keeps working
Yes. Without this no “train” could run.
He must feed the quarrels that drive progress
Not quite. The article says: He must control both his anger at others and his wish to run away, so that society keeps working.
He must work harder than everyone else
Not quite. The article says: He must control both his anger at others and his wish to run away, so that society keeps working.
He must keep others at a safe distance
Not quite. The article says: He must control both his anger at others and his wish to run away, so that society keeps working.
questions.rationale: “Just as the engine driver controls both the fire which drives the engine and his own desire to escape from it, so must the individual in society tame both his own fury and a desire to simply run away.”

questions.q: What keeps a family together through daily disagreements, and what must do the same work in a society?
options: In both, the absence of any differences
Not quite. The article says: In a family, bonds of love; in society, a conscious, reasoned decision to agree to disagree.
In a family, bonds of love; in society, a conscious, reasoned decision to agree to disagree
Well read. One is instinctive, the other a deliberate effort.
In a family, the father’s authority; in society, the law
Not quite. The article says: In a family, bonds of love; in society, a conscious, reasoned decision to agree to disagree.
In a family, shared money; in society, shared trade
Not quite. The article says: In a family, bonds of love; in society, a conscious, reasoned decision to agree to disagree.
questions.rationale: “While it is an emotional bond that keeps families from disintegrating, it is a rational effort which cements society.”

questions.q: The article contrasts the outlook “Islam is true” with “I am true.” What does each produce?
options: The first, pride; the second, humility
Not quite. The article says: The first, fear of God; the second, a false sense of superiority.
Both produce the same character
Not quite. The article says: The first, fear of God; the second, a false sense of superiority.
The first, fear of God; the second, a false sense of superiority
Correct. The article sees in this the difference between rise and decline.
The first, doubt; the second, certainty
Not quite. The article says: The first, fear of God; the second, a false sense of superiority.
questions.rationale: “The first conception engenders the fear of God. The second promotes a false sense of superiority.”

questions.q: How does a God-conscious person see each evening and each morning, according to the article?
options: Evening as a likeness of the first call of the Day of Judgement, morning as the rising before God
Yes. Going to bed is like lying in the grave; waking, like resurrection.
Evening as rest earned, morning as work owed
Not quite. The article says: Evening as a likeness of the first call of the Day of Judgement, morning as the rising before God.
Evening as loss, morning as gain
Not quite. The article says: Evening as a likeness of the first call of the Day of Judgement, morning as the rising before God.
Both as matters of no meaning
Not quite. The article says: Evening as a likeness of the first call of the Day of Judgement, morning as the rising before God.
questions.rationale: “Every evening therefore is an illustration of the scenario after the first call of the Day of Judgement. Every morning is an illustration of the scenario of the second call.”

questions.q: The musk deer runs about searching for a scent that comes from itself. What does the article say this shows about happiness?
options: It belongs to animals more than to people
Not quite. The article says: It is an inner state of mind, not something to be found outside.
It can be found only by travelling
Not quite. The article says: It is an inner state of mind, not something to be found outside.
It depends on what others think of us
Not quite. The article says: It is an inner state of mind, not something to be found outside.
It is an inner state of mind, not something to be found outside
Right. Contentment with need, not pursuit of greed.
questions.rationale: “Man searches for happiness outside of him, although happiness is inside him… Happiness is an internal phenomenon, it is not an external achievement.”

questions.article: Living in the Great Blessings of God
questions.q: After naming animals for riding, the Quran adds: “He creates what you do not know.” How does the article understand these words?
options: As referring to creatures of the deep sea
Not quite. The article says: As pointing ahead to means still to come, such as modern industrial civilisation.
As describing the angels
Not quite. The article says: As pointing ahead to means still to come, such as modern industrial civilisation.
As pointing ahead to means still to come, such as modern industrial civilisation
Yes. It was present in nature in potential form.
As a reminder that knowledge is forbidden
Not quite. The article says: As pointing ahead to means still to come, such as modern industrial civilisation.
questions.rationale: “This blessing is the industrial civilization which was present in nature in the potential sense at the time of the revelation of the Quran.”

questions.q: When a negative thought arises, why does the article insist on dealing with it at once?
options: Left alone, it sinks beyond conscious control and becomes part of one’s personality
Well reasoned. Anger forgiven at once does not turn into revenge.
It grows weaker with time, so haste wastes effort
Not quite. The article says: Left alone, it sinks beyond conscious control and becomes part of one’s personality.
Others will notice it
Not quite. The article says: Left alone, it sinks beyond conscious control and becomes part of one’s personality.
It will be forgotten by morning anyway
Not quite. The article says: Left alone, it sinks beyond conscious control and becomes part of one’s personality.
questions.rationale: “If there is a delay in this process… it will become such an integral part of the personality and even if man wants to detach it from his personality, he will not be able to do so.”

questions.q: A crime in Delhi was uncovered months later from the ashes of the dead man. What larger truth does the article draw?
options: The police always find the guilty
Not quite. The article says: Every deed leaves a record that cannot be wiped away, for the world is of God’s making.
Only great crimes are ever recorded
Not quite. The article says: Every deed leaves a record that cannot be wiped away, for the world is of God’s making.
Science has made crime impossible
Not quite. The article says: Every deed leaves a record that cannot be wiped away, for the world is of God’s making.
Every deed leaves a record that cannot be wiped away, for the world is of God’s making
Exactly. We are free to act, not to erase.
questions.rationale: “As soon as a deed is done, it gets affixed to the ‘cosmic record’ and no one can ever rub it off thereafter.”
